glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Psalm 117 calls every nation to praise the LORD because His merciful kindness toward His people is great and His truth endures forever.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: The shortest psalm in the Bible belongs to the Hallel (Psalms 113–118), a group of praise psalms used in Israel’s worship. In two verses it moves from a worldwide summons to the reason for it and back to praise.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Psalm 117:1 — A Call to All Nations to Praise the LORD

  • Psalm 117:2 — His Merciful Kindness and Enduring Truth

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “For His merciful kindness is great toward us, And the truth of the LORD endures forever. Praise the LORD!” (Psalm 117:2, NKJV)

cards.title: Author
cards.html: Psalm 117 has no title, and Scripture does not name its author. It stands in Book Five of the Psalms (Psalms 107–150) among the Hallel psalms. Some Hebrew manuscripts join it to a neighboring psalm, but it has long been read as a complete song of its own.

cards.title: Occasion
cards.html: The psalm names no historical event, and none should be assigned to it. Jewish tradition records that the Hallel psalms were sung at the great feasts, including Passover, so the hymn Jesus and His disciples sang before going to the Mount of Olives was most likely drawn from this collection (Matthew 26:30).

cards.title: Psalm Type
cards.html: A hymn of praise in its simplest form. Verse 1 issues the call, verse 2 gives the reason with the word “For,” and the closing “Praise the LORD!” (117:2) returns to the call.

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Israel’s shortest song has the widest reach. “Praise the LORD, all you Gentiles! Laud Him, all you peoples!” (117:1). Israel does not ask the nations to admire its God from a distance; it calls them to worship Him. God’s purpose for the whole world was being sung in Israel’s own hymnbook.

The reason is what God has shown Israel: “His merciful kindness is great toward us” (117:2). The word for “is great” carries the sense of strength that prevails, so God’s love is pictured as a force that overcomes. His “truth,” His faithfulness, “endures forever” (117:2). The pair recalls how the LORD described Himself to Moses as “abounding in goodness and truth” (Exodus 34:6). Israel’s testimony to that steady love becomes the nations’ reason to sing.

Paul quotes the psalm’s first verse in Romans 15:11 to show that Gentiles glorifying God for His mercy was part of God’s plan from the start, fulfilled in Christ, who came to confirm the promises made to the fathers (Romans 15:8–9). Throughout, the psalm grounds praise in who God is.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Psalm 117:1 — A Call to All Nations to Praise the LORD

The psalm opens with two parallel commands that reach beyond Israel to every Gentile nation and every people. To “praise” and to “laud” the LORD both mean to speak His worth aloud.

Psalm 117:2 — His Merciful Kindness and Enduring Truth

The word “For” gives the reason for the call: the LORD’s merciful kindness toward His people is strong and His truth lasts forever. The closing “Praise the LORD!” frames the psalm, ending where it began.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Psalm 117 shows that God’s heart for the nations is old. When He called Abraham, He promised blessing to all the families of the earth (Genesis 12:3), and here Israel is already inviting those families to worship. Believers from the nations who praise God today are answering a call Israel sang centuries before Christ.

The psalm also shows that worship has a foundation. The nations are told to praise because God’s love prevails and His faithfulness does not wear out. Praise built on His character can continue when circumstances change, because He does not.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The nations called to worship. Every Gentile nation and people is summoned to praise the LORD (117:1; Romans 15:11).

Israel’s testimony. The mercy shown “toward us” becomes the reason the nations should praise (117:2).

Love that prevails. God’s merciful kindness is great, strong enough to overcome (117:2).

Faithfulness that lasts. The truth of the LORD endures forever (117:2; Psalm 100:5).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Gentiles and peoples. Hebrew goyim and ummim, the nations beyond Israel. The two terms together leave no people out (117:1).

Laud. To praise or commend aloud, a word of spoken celebration (117:1).

Merciful kindness. Hebrew hesed, God’s steadfast, faithful love toward His people, loyal and dependable (117:2).

Is great. Hebrew gavar, to be strong or to prevail. God’s love is not fragile; it wins out (117:2).

Truth. Hebrew emet, firmness and reliability. It speaks of God’s faithfulness to His word as well as the accuracy of what He says (117:2).

Praise the LORD. Hebrew hallelu-Yah, the familiar Hallelujah, a call to praise Yah, a short form of the LORD’s personal name (117:2).

culture.title: We are a Tabernacle of David
culture.statement: We were created to delight the Father and host His presence. As we embrace His ways, our lives become continual offerings of praise—both personally and together. We live with unhindered access to God, ministering to Him first and carrying His presence wherever we go. As His dwelling is restored among us, we become a people through whom the nations are drawn to seek the Lord.
culture.label: Living It in Psalms 117
culture.html:
“Praise the LORD, all you Gentiles! Laud Him, all you peoples!” (Psalm 117:1).

Israel's worship was never intended to be limited to Israel. Even as God's people praised Him, they called the nations to join them. Worship was both an offering to the LORD and an invitation for others to know and honor Him.

This reflects the heart of a Tabernacle of David. We minister to the Lord because He is worthy of our love and praise, but His heart is for the nations. We want our worship and the life of God's presence among us to draw others to Him. Our desire is not simply to enjoy His presence ourselves, but to see people everywhere come to know the God we worship.

culture.title: We Stand with Israel
culture.statement: We love what the Lord loves. The Lord loves Israel, and we love Israel. We take seriously the Lord’s promise to bless those who bless Israel, and curse those who curse Israel.
culture.label: Living It in Psalms 117
culture.html:
“For His merciful kindness is great toward us, And the truth of the LORD endures forever” (Psalm 117:2).

The nations are commanded to praise the LORD because of His merciful kindness toward “us,” referring first to Israel. This is remarkable. The Gentiles are invited to worship God because of His enduring love and faithfulness to His people.

Paul explains this connection in Romans 15:8–11. Christ came to confirm God's promises to Israel's fathers so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy. God's faithfulness to Israel became the means through which His mercy reached the nations.

We stand with Israel because we love what God loves and honor His purposes for His people. We do not forget the people through whom God brought His promises and ultimately His Son into the world. As Gentile believers, we have particular reason to rejoice in God's enduring faithfulness to Israel, because through Christ that faithfulness has brought mercy to us.

culture.title: Unity
culture.statement: We choose submission to the Holy Spirit and one another over our personal preferences, giftings, and anointings. Our hearts’ desires are to know God and walk in His ways. We understand that the greatest blessings and anointings are found when we are united together in Christ.
culture.label: Living It in Psalms 117
culture.html:
“Praise the LORD, all you Gentiles! Laud Him, all you peoples!” (Psalm 117:1).

The psalm calls people from every nation and background to worship the same LORD. Though separated by nationality, language, and culture, they are united in the One they are called to praise.

Paul quotes this psalm in Romans 15:11 within his appeal for believers to receive one another just as Christ received them (Romans 15:7). Through Christ, Jews and Gentiles are brought together and united in worship of the same God.

This speaks directly to our culture of unity. Our unity is not built on having the same backgrounds, personalities, preferences, or traditions. It comes from belonging to Jesus Christ and sharing a common desire to know, honor and worship Him. We welcome and receive those whom Christ has received, making room for people from every background to worship and pursue the Lord together.

sections.title: A Call to All Nations to Praise the LORD
His Merciful Kindness and Enduring Truth

groups.title: Praise the LORD, All You Nations

items.title: Call, Cause, Call
items.html: The psalm moves in three steps: a call (“Praise the LORD”), a cause (“For His merciful kindness… and the truth of the LORD”), and the call again (“Praise the LORD!”). The small word “for” holds it together. Biblical praise is a response to what is true about God. Take away verse 2, and verse 1 is a shout with nothing behind it. If your worship rises and falls with the music or with your emotions, go back to the “for.”
items.q: The psalm moves in three steps: a call (“Praise the LORD”), a cause (“For His merciful kindness… and the truth of the LORD”), and the call again (“Praise the LORD!”).

items.title: A Psalm That Asks for Nothing
items.html: Psalm 117 has no petition, complaint, or plea for rescue. In a book of Psalms full of cries for help, this psalm asks God for nothing. It tells the nations to praise Him and gives the reasons: His merciful kindness and His truth. Much of our prayer is rightly asking. We can also come into His presence simply to thank Him, enjoy Him, and declare His goodness. Try spending part of your prayer time this week with no requests at all, only praise for who He is and what He has already done. If God never gave you another thing, would what He has already shown you be enough to praise Him?
items.q: If God never gave you another thing, would what He has already shown you be enough to praise Him?

items.title: Nations Rise and Fall; His Truth Remains
items.html: Psalm 117 calls every nation to praise the LORD because His truth endures forever. Israel watched Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome rise and fall, and each of them claimed authority over many peoples. Every one of them is gone. “The grass withers, the flower fades, But the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Rulers make promises they cannot keep, and whole cultures change, but God does not change with them. Whoever is in power and whatever the headlines say, the truth of the LORD will outlast all of it.
items.q: Psalm 117 calls every nation to praise the LORD because His truth endures forever.

items.title: What the Nations See in God’s People
items.html: The nations are told to praise God because of His merciful kindness “toward us.” The evidence they are given is what God has done among His people. Israel’s life was meant to show the world what God is like. The same is true of the church. Jesus said, “By this all will know that you are My disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). When people look at us, they should see the mercy and truth this psalm praises. When God’s people are harsh, divided or dishonest, they make His mercy and truth harder to believe. What does the way we treat one another tell people about God?
items.q: What does the way we treat one another tell people about God?

items.title: From “My Voice” to “All You Peoples.”
items.html: Psalm 117 sits right after a very personal psalm. Psalm 116 begins, “I love the LORD, because He has heard my voice” (116:1). By its end, the psalmist is praising God “in the presence of all His people” (116:18). Then Psalm 117 calls all the nations to praise. Read together, the praise moves outward: from one rescued person, to God’s people, to the whole world. Personal experience of God’s mercy should widen our hearts toward others. The person who can honestly say “He heard my voice” is the one most ready to say, “Praise Him, all you peoples.” Has what God has done for me made me more concerned for people who do not know Him yet?
items.q: Has what God has done for me made me more concerned for people who do not know Him yet?

items.title: Many Tongues, One Song
items.html: Psalm 117 calls the nations and peoples to praise the LORD. At Babel, God scattered the peoples by confusing their languages (Genesis 11:7–9). At Pentecost, people from many nations heard the wonderful works of God, each “in our own language” (Acts 2:8, 11). In Revelation, the redeemed are still “of all nations, tribes, peoples, and tongues” (Revelation 7:9). God brings the nations together in praise and keeps their languages. A church where people worship in more than one language is a small picture of what heaven will sound like. Heaven’s worship brings together every people on earth to sing to one Lamb. Can I enjoy worship that sounds different from mine?
items.q: Can I enjoy worship that sounds different from mine?

items.title: A House of Prayer for All Nations
items.html: The same week Jesus likely sang the Hallel, He drove the buyers and sellers out of the temple, quoting Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Mark 11:17). The trading was most likely in the outer court, the one place Gentiles could come to pray. The place where the nations should have been praising God had been crowded out by business. Jesus cleared it, likely sang the psalm that summons the nations, and went to the cross where the dividing wall came down (Ephesians 2:14). Churches can crowd out the nations the same way without noticing, filling the room with programs, preferences, and insider language until there’s no space left for the outsider. Jesus is still clearing that court. What in our church might make it harder for an outsider to come near to God?
items.q: What in our church might make it harder for an outsider to come near to God?

items.title: Hallelujah: The Exodus Song Handed to the Nations
items.html:
The psalm ends with the Hebrew expression Hallelujah, “Praise Yah,” using the short form of God’s name. That short form first appears in Israel’s song at the Red Sea: “The LORD [Yah] is my strength and song, And He has become my salvation” (Exodus 15:2). The name the nations are called to praise is the name Israel first sang after God brought them through the sea. In the New Testament, “Alleluia” appears only in Revelation 19, rising again and again from “a great multitude in heaven” (19:1, 3, 4, 6). Earlier in Revelation, the victorious sing “the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb,” declaring, “All nations shall come and worship before You” (Revelation 15:3–4). For centuries Israel sang this psalm to the nations. One day the nations will sing it back.

Psalm 117. The whole psalm rests on two truths about God: His merciful kindness toward His people is great, and His truth endures forever. God wants me to know His heart and character. I can trust Him completely because He is always true to Himself and to His promises.

What God may be saying: “See how great My love is toward you. You can trust My heart, rest in My faithfulness, and draw near to Me without fear. Let what you have seen of My love and faithfulness fill your heart with praise.”
items.q: The psalm ends with the Hebrew expression Hallelujah , “Praise Yah,” using the short form of God’s name.

1.brief: The shortest psalm in the Bible opens with a call for every nation and people on earth to praise the LORD. Paul later quotes this verse to show that God always planned for the Gentiles to join in worshiping Him through Christ.
1.explain:
"Praise the LORD, all you Gentiles!"

"Praise" translates halal, which means to praise, celebrate, or boast in someone. It is the root of Hallelujah. "The LORD" stands for God's personal name, the name He revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14–15). The nations are called to worship Israel's own God by name.

In this setting, "Gentiles" translates the Hebrew word for nations and points to the peoples of the world beyond Israel. These were nations that bowed to idols and often fought against God's people, yet a psalm sung in Israel's worship invites every one of them to praise the LORD. God told Abraham at the very beginning, "And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Genesis 12:3). He chose Israel as the people through whom His blessing would reach every nation.

"Laud Him, all you peoples!"

"Laud" translates shabach, a less common word meaning to praise, commend, or declare someone's greatness. "Peoples" is another word for the nations. As Hebrew poetry often does, the second line repeats the first in different words. The two verbs overlap in meaning, and the repetition makes the call emphatic and extends it to every people on earth.

Paul quotes this verse in Romans 15:11. He was writing to a church of Jewish and Gentile believers, urging them to "receive one another, just as Christ also received us, to the glory of God" (Romans 15:7). He gathers several Old Testament passages, including this one, to show that Gentiles worshiping the God of Israel through Christ was God's plan from the start. Israel had been singing about it all along.
1.notes:
(Technical & Expository Notes)

Psalm 117 belongs to Psalms 113–118, which Jewish tradition calls the Hallel, from the Hebrew word for "praise." This group is often called the "Egyptian Hallel" because it celebrates God's rescue of Israel from Egypt (Psalm 114 retells the Exodus directly). By New Testament times these psalms were sung at Israel's great festivals, including Passover. Early Jewish sources describe the Hallel divided in two at the Passover meal, with the first part sung before the meal and the rest, including Psalm 117, sung after it.

That custom gives added depth to Matthew 26:30: "And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives." The Gospels do not name the hymn, but given Passover practice it was most likely the closing portion of the Hallel. If so, on the night before His death Jesus sang this call for all nations to praise the LORD, along with Psalm 118's words about the rejected stone becoming the chief cornerstone.

hearing.observe: The people called here are the “Gentiles,” the nations beyond Israel. These nations bowed to idols and often fought against God’s people. Yet Israel’s own song invites every one of them, saying “all” twice, to praise “the LORD,” God’s personal name, the name He revealed to Moses. The second line repeats the call: “Laud Him,” meaning commend Him and declare His greatness. This was God’s heart from the beginning, when He told Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3). Paul quotes this verse to a church of Jewish and Gentile believers, urging them to “receive one another, just as Christ also received us” (Romans 15:7–11). Israel had been singing about that welcome all along.
hearing.hear:
Most of us reading this are among the “Gentiles” this psalm was calling. We were once far from God, and now we are invited to praise Him by name. The invitation was being sung over us long before we knew Him.

Because Christ has received people from every nation into one family of praise, I can gladly receive believers whose background, language, and culture differ from mine. Our voices belong together in the same song.

hearing.observe: Psalm 117 belongs to the Hallel (Psalms 113–118), the psalms Israel sang at Passover. Early Jewish sources place it among those sung after the meal. Matthew records that after the Passover meal, Jesus and His disciples “had sung a hymn” and then went out to the Mount of Olives (Matthew 26:30). The Gospels do not name the hymn, but it was most likely this closing part of the Hallel. On the night before His death, Jesus probably sang this call for all nations to praise the LORD. Then He went out toward the cross that would make the call possible to answer.
hearing.hear: Jesus likely sang this invitation on His way to the cross. Only days earlier He had said that when He was lifted up, He would “draw all peoples” to Himself (John 12:32), and He endured the cross “for the joy that was set before Him” (Hebrews 12:2). I am one of the people He went to the cross to gather. When I praise the LORD, I am answering a call that cost Him His life. My praise can begin with thanks for that.

reflections.title: Jonah Knew the Same Mercy and Wanted to Keep It for Himself
reflections.html: The nations had enslaved Israel in Egypt and attacked them for generations. Yet the psalm Israel sang at Passover calls those same nations to praise the LORD. Jonah knew that mercy well. He prayed, “I know that You are a gracious and merciful God, slow to anger and abundant in lovingkindness” (Jonah 4:2). “Lovingkindness” translates the Hebrew word hesed, the same word as “merciful kindness” in Psalm 117:2. That is exactly why Jonah was angry. He did not want God’s mercy reaching Nineveh, the great city of Israel’s enemy. It is possible to love God’s mercy for ourselves and resent it for others. Most of us have a Nineveh: someone who hurt us, a group we have written off, or a nation we see in the news as the enemy. Do we want God’s mercy to reach them too?
reflections.q: Do we want God’s mercy to reach them too?

reflections.title: “All You Peoples.”
reflections.html: The psalm says “all” twice: “all you Gentiles” and “all you peoples.” In heaven that call is answered by people “out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). Paul quoted this psalm to a church divided into groups (Romans 15:7–11). It is possible to rejoice that God welcomed us while quietly keeping certain people at a distance. Sometimes it is prejudice, in how we think and talk about people of another race, country, or language. Sometimes it is a clique, the same circle at every church gathering while others stand at the edges. A prejudiced heart is not God’s heart. God’s heart reaches all peoples, and ours should too. Is there anyone I am keeping at a distance whom God has welcomed?
reflections.q: Is there anyone I am keeping at a distance whom God has welcomed?

reflections.title: The Psalm Paul Used to Heal a Divided Church
reflections.html: Paul quotes Psalm 117:1 in Romans 15:11 while writing to a church quarreling over food, holy days, and matters of conscience (Romans 14–15). The groups were largely Jewish and Gentile believers. Paul wanted them to glorify God together “with one mind and one mouth” (Romans 15:6). He showed them from the Scriptures, including this psalm, that God had always intended Jews and Gentiles to praise Him together. At the cross Christ broke down the wall between them and put their hostility to death, creating “one new man from the two” (Ephesians 2:15–16). If Christ has put the hostility to death, His people must not revive it.
reflections.q: Paul quotes Psalm 117:1 in Romans 15:11 while writing to a church quarreling over food, holy days, and matters of conscience (Romans 14–15).

reflections.title: Giving Jesus His Inheritance
reflections.html: The first time the Psalms mention the nations, they are raging “against the LORD and against His Anointed” (Psalm 2:1–2). In that same psalm God says to His Son, “Ask of Me, and I will give You the nations for Your inheritance” (Psalm 2:8). Psalm 117 does not mention Psalm 2, but it calls those same nations to praise the LORD. Read together, the two psalms show the nations moving from rage to praise as the Son receives what was promised Him. When we pray for the lost and bring people to Jesus, we are joining the Father in giving His Son His inheritance. Who can I pray for by name this week?
reflections.q: Who can I pray for by name this week?

reflections.title: The Spirit Puts Praise in Gentile Mouths
reflections.html: Psalm 117 calls the nations to praise a God most of them did not know. The New Testament shows how that call was answered: by the Holy Spirit. Just after quoting this psalm, Paul describes his ministry as presenting “the offering of the Gentiles… sanctified by the Holy Spirit” (Romans 15:16). When the Spirit fell on Cornelius’s household, those Gentile believers were heard to “speak with tongues and magnify God” (Acts 10:46). The same Spirit gives praise to God’s people today. When my heart feels dry in worship, I can ask the Holy Spirit to fill me and put praise in my mouth again.
reflections.q: Psalm 117 calls the nations to praise a God most of them did not know.

reflections.title: Two Heralds Calling the Nations
reflections.html: The word for “peoples” in this verse is rare in Hebrew, but it appears often in the Aramaic chapters of Daniel. Nebuchadnezzar’s herald uses it to summon the world: “To you it is commanded, O peoples, nations, and languages.” Whoever would not bow to the golden image was thrown into the furnace (Daniel 3:4–6). Psalm 117 also calls the nations to worship, and the reason it gives is God’s merciful kindness. Later, after God humbled him, Nebuchadnezzar used the same verb as this psalm’s “laud”: “I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven, all of whose works are truth” (Daniel 4:37). The king who built the furnace ended up giving God the praise this psalm calls for. Earthly rulers have often demanded worship through fear, while the LORD calls the nations to Himself with His mercy.
reflections.q: The word for “peoples” in this verse is rare in Hebrew, but it appears often in the Aramaic chapters of Daniel.

2.brief: The reason all nations should praise God is that His faithful love toward His people is great and His truth, meaning His reliability in keeping His promises, lasts forever. The psalm closes as it began, with "Praise the LORD," showing that God's steady love and faithfulness are the heart of all true worship.
2.explain:
"For His merciful kindness is great toward us,"

"For" gives the reason the nations should praise the LORD. "Merciful kindness" translates hesed, God's loyal, steadfast love: love that keeps showing kindness because of a commitment already made. God had bound Himself to Israel with the promise that He would be their God and they would be His people, and hesed is the love that stays true to that promise even when His people fail.

"Is great" translates gabar, which speaks of strength and prevailing power. The same verb describes the floodwaters that "prevailed" over the earth (Genesis 7:18). Here it emphasizes the greatness of God's merciful kindness toward His people.

"Us" most naturally refers to Israel, the people who had experienced His kindness firsthand. Yet every nation is called to praise God for what He has done for them, because His promise to Abraham meant that His blessing on Israel would reach all the families of the earth. Paul makes the same connection just before quoting this psalm, explaining that Christ came "to confirm the promises made to the fathers, and that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy" (Romans 15:8–9).

"And the truth of the LORD endures forever."

"Truth" translates emet, which describes what is firm and reliable. Used of God, it means His faithfulness: He does what He says. When the LORD revealed His character to Moses, He called Himself "abounding in goodness and truth" (Exodus 34:6), using the same two Hebrew words found here. His love moves Him to make His promises, and His faithfulness guarantees He will keep them.

"Endures forever" means His faithfulness lasts through every generation. The promises God made to Abraham centuries before this psalm still stood, and they remain trustworthy today.

"Praise the LORD!"

In Hebrew this is Hallelujah. The psalm ends with the same call to praise that opened it, and between the two calls stand two truths about God: His great kindness and His lasting faithfulness. The nations are called to praise Him for His steady love and dependable promises, shown to His people and offered through them to the world.
2.notes:
(Technical & Expository Notes)

The NKJV follows the Hebrew arrangement, where the closing "Praise the LORD" (Hallelujah) ends Psalm 117. In the Greek arrangement represented by the Rahlfs edition and the New English Translation of the Septuagint, this psalm is numbered 116 and the following psalm, Hebrew Psalm 118, is numbered 117. That following Greek psalm begins with Hallelujah. The opening and closing praise of Psalm 117 in the NKJV follow the Hebrew arrangement.

hearing.observe: The psalm gives a reason for its praise, and the reason is who God is. “Merciful kindness” translates the Hebrew word hesed, God’s loyal, steadfast love. “Is great” means strong or prevailing, and the same Hebrew word describes the floodwaters that “prevailed” over the earth (Genesis 7:18). “Truth” means His reliability in keeping His word, and it endures forever. These are the same two words God used when He revealed Himself to Moses: “abounding in goodness and truth” (Exodus 34:6). His love moves Him to make His promises, and His faithfulness keeps them.
hearing.hear: My praise rests on who God is, so I can praise Him on hard days as well as good ones. His love toward me is great, and His faithfulness will last through every generation after mine. The word that described the floodwaters prevailing over the earth now describes His merciful kindness prevailing over my life. When I come to the last word of this psalm, Hallelujah, I can answer it gladly.

hearing.observe: “Us” most naturally refers to Israel, the people who had experienced God’s kindness firsthand. Yet the psalm calls the nations to praise God for that kindness. Paul explains why just before he quotes Psalm 117. Christ came “to confirm the promises made to the fathers, and that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy” (Romans 15:8–9). In the same verse Paul says Christ came “for the truth of God,” so he uses the psalm’s two words, truth and mercy. God made promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He kept them by sending Christ through Israel, and through Christ His mercy reached the nations.
hearing.hear: The mercy I have received came to me because God kept promises He made long before I was born. He was faithful to Israel, and that faithfulness reached me. I can thank Him for keeping His word to Israel, and I can trust Him to keep His word to me.

reflections.title: How Great Is His Mercy?
reflections.html: Psalm 117:2 says His merciful kindness “is great toward us.” Psalm 103 uses the same two Hebrew words together and gives them a measure: “For as the heavens are high above the earth, So great is His mercy toward those who fear Him” (Psalm 103:11). David then says what that mercy does: “As far as the east is from the west, So far has He removed our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12). Many believers know God has forgiven them but still carry the weight of what they have done. God’s mercy toward His people is greater than their sin. Is there something I keep carrying that His mercy has already removed?
reflections.q: Is there something I keep carrying that His mercy has already removed?

reflections.title: Merciful Is the First Word
reflections.html: When God revealed His character to Moses, the first thing He said about Himself was “The LORD, the LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abounding in goodness and truth” (Exodus 34:6). It is possible to believe we are forgiven and still picture the Father as harsh, as if He forgave us reluctantly. God describes Himself first as merciful and gracious, and Psalm 117 says His merciful kindness toward His people is great. I can come to Him without fear. In Christ, the Father I approach is full of mercy.
reflections.q: When God revealed His character to Moses, the first thing He said about Himself was “The LORD, the LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abounding in goodness and truth” (Exodus 34:6).

reflections.title: From Outsiders to Insiders
reflections.html: Psalm 117 speaks to the Gentiles as “you” in verse 1, then says God’s mercy is great toward “us,” His people Israel, in verse 2. The Gentiles begin the psalm on the outside. In Christ, those who were once “far off” have been brought near by His blood (Ephesians 2:13). They are now “fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). Some believers still feel like outsiders, at church or before God. If you are in Christ, you belong in God’s household. You can join Israel in saying, “His merciful kindness is great toward us.”
reflections.q: Psalm 117 speaks to the Gentiles as “you” in verse 1, then says God’s mercy is great toward “us,”

reflections.title: Can You Praise God for Someone Else’s Blessing?
reflections.html:
The nations are told to praise God for mercy He showed to Israel. The Queen of Sheba did exactly that when she visited Solomon: “Blessed be the LORD your God… Because the LORD has loved Israel forever” (1 Kings 10:9). She praised God for His love toward another people. That means thanking God sincerely when He answers someone else’s prayer, heals someone else’s child, or blesses someone else’s ministry, before He has done the same for us. Praise like that keeps envy from taking root. Can we thank God for what He is doing in someone else’s life?

[Christ & Life] Mercy and Truth with a Face. Psalm 117:2 praises God for His merciful kindness and His truth, expressed in the Hebrew words hesed and emet. Moses heard those same two words when he asked to see God’s glory and the LORD passed by, proclaiming Himself “abounding in goodness and truth” (Exodus 33:18; 34:6). Moses heard God described, but he was not allowed to see His face. John describes Jesus in words that echo that moment: “We beheld His glory… full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The mercy and truth this psalm praises are seen in Jesus. Jesus is the face of mercy and truth.
reflections.q: The nations are told to praise God for mercy He showed to Israel.

reflections.title: Faithfulness With No Expiration Date
reflections.html: “The truth of the LORD endures forever.” The psalm just before this one says, “I said in my haste, ‘All men are liars’” (Psalm 116:11). In his distress the psalmist felt that no one could be trusted. At Passover these two psalms were sung one after the other, so the next thing Israel sang was that the truth of the LORD endures forever. Paul draws on that same verse: “Let God be true but every man a liar” (Romans 3:4). People will disappoint us, and promises will be broken. God’s word still stands. Have I let disappointment with people make me slow to trust God?
reflections.q: Have I let disappointment with people make me slow to trust God?

reflections.title: The Truth That Says “Amen.”
reflections.html: The Hebrew word emet, translated “truth,” comes from the same root as amen. Both describe what is firm and faithful, something that can bear weight. Isaiah calls the LORD “the God of truth,” literally “the God of amen” (Isaiah 65:16). Jesus calls Himself “the Amen, the Faithful and True Witness” (Revelation 3:14), and in Him all God’s promises are “Yes” and “Amen” (2 Corinthians 1:20). Faith means leaning my full weight on the One who will not give way. Every time I end a prayer with “Amen,” I am saying that God and His Word can be trusted.
reflections.q: The Hebrew word emet , translated “truth,” comes from the same root as amen .
